title: Setting up the shaving horse
subtitle: How to position, clamp, and work at the shaving horse
excerpt: The shaving horse is the workbench for drawknife and spokeshave work. Getting the seat height, clamp adjustment, and body position right before starting work is faster than correcting problems mid-project. This technique covers setup from scratch.

glossaryTerms.definition: A foot-operated clamp bench for holding work while using a drawknife or spokeshave.
A two-handled blade drawn toward the user to shave or shape wood. Bevel up gives a shallow, slicing cut; bevel down gives deeper material removal.

content.text: The
shaving horse

is a foot-operated clamp bench. Pressing the foot treadle down drives a clamping jaw down onto the work; releasing the treadle opens the clamp. The worker sits astride the bench, feet on the treadle, both hands on the drawknife. Getting the setup right is the whole technique: once the horse is adjusted for the worker and the work, the clamping and cutting follow naturally.
Before you start.
The drawknife must be sharp. At the shaving horse, a dull drawknife requires more force, which means less control over the stopping point.
The clamp jaw must lock the work before any drawknife stroke. Never begin a stroke on a piece that is not fully clamped.
The drawknife blade must stop before it reaches the thighs. Set the clamp height so that the end of the stroke brings the blade to rest 15 to 20 cm from the body.
Stable footing: the shaving horse must sit on firm, level ground. It should not rock or slide.
Parts of the shaving horse
Seat: the long central beam the worker sits on. Ideally 45 to 50 cm from the ground for an average adult.
Work deck: the horizontal platform in front of the seat where the work rests.
Clamp arm and jaw: the pivoting arm that clamps the work against the deck when the treadle is pressed.
Treadle: the foot bar that pivots the clamp arm. Pressing down clamps; releasing opens.
Adjusting for the worker

Sit on the bench with feet resting flat on the treadle. The treadle should be reachable with the feet flat and the knees at a comfortable angle, not stretched out. On most shaving horses the clamp height is adjustable by a peg or a threaded bolt. Set the clamp height so that a piece of round stock 30 to 40 mm in diameter is held firmly at the height of the work deck surface.
Clamping the work
Place the work on the deck between the jaw and the deck surface. Press the treadle: the jaw drops and grips the work. Test the grip before picking up the
drawknife

: push the work with one hand. If it moves, the jaw is not gripping firmly. Adjust the clamp height: a piece held too low in the clamp will lever out under drawknife pressure rather than being held firm.
Body position during cutting

Sit with the back straight and the elbows slightly bent when the drawknife is at the start of the stroke. The stroke ends with the elbows near the body. The distance from start to end of stroke is 25 to 35 cm for most people. Do not lean back during the stroke; the power comes from the arms and core, not from falling backward.
Repositioning the work

Release the treadle to open the clamp. The work is now free to rotate or slide. Reposition with one hand while the foot is off the treadle. Press the treadle again to re-clamp before picking up the drawknife. This open-clamp to reposition to re-clamp sequence is the natural rhythm of shaving-horse work; do not try to hold the work down by hand while cutting with the drawknife in the other hand.
